newsitem.title: USA: IRS criticized for lax security of taxpayer data.
newsitem.headline: IRS criticized for lax security of taxpayer data.

text.p: The Internal Revenue Service has weaknesses in security, inadequate monitoring for employees snooping into taxpayer files and thousands of missing data tapes, a government report said Tuesday.

The General Accounting Office (GAO), which conducts investigations for Congress, said the IRS "continues to have serious weaknesses in the controls used to safeguard IRS computer systems, facilities, and taxpayer data."

The GAO conducted on-site reviews at five IRS facilities and found they could not account for about 6,400 missing data tapes and cartridges that could contain taxpayer data. The number of lost data tapes per facility ranged from a low of 41 to a high of 5,946, the GAO said.
"In addition, printouts containing taxpayer data were left unprotected and unattended in open areas of two facilities where they could be compromised," the GAO said.

Sen. John Glenn, an Ohio Democrat who released the report, said the IRS investigated 1,515 employees for unauthorised browsing of taxpayer files in fiscal years 1994 and 1995, and of those only 23 resulted in employees being fired.
"That doesn't sound like zero tolerance to me," Glenn said, referring to a stated IRS policy of "zero tolerance" for unauthorised browsing.
"The bottom line is the IRS really has no idea how extensive the problem is, how often browsing is detected, how many times employees browse, how many accounts they may have accessed," Glenn said.
The GAO said despite the attention to the issue of unauthorised browsing of taxpayer data by IRS employees, the tax collection agency was not effectively addressing it.
A system that IRS developed to monitor and detect browsing on the primary computer system that its employees use to access taxpayer accounts has shortcomings, the GAO said.
The IRS was also inconsistent in reviewing incidents of browsing and penalties, the report said.

Glenn said he was introducing legislation aimed at closing a legal loophole that allows criminal prosecution of unauthorised browsing by IRS employees of taxpayer files only if the information is passed on to someone else or used for criminal purposes.
The chairman of the House tax-writing committee is also introducing legislation aimed at installing criminal penalties for browsing.
House Speaker Newt Gingrich, a Georgia Republican, said he hoped legislation that "stops IRS agents from misusing their power" would pass Congress and be signed into law by the president.

The GAO report found "many weaknesses" in the internal audit or internal security functions at the IRS facilities it reviewed and said two of the sites had not audited their operations within the last five years.
None of the five facilities had "comprehensive disaster recovery plans" in case of such events as electrical power failures, earthquakes, floods and fires, the GAO said.

A Treasury Department response included in the GAO report said the agency has taken steps to address concerns raised in the report and stressed the IRS does not tolerate unauthorised browsing by its employees.
The IRS uses automated information systems to process over 200 million taxpayer returns and collect more than $1 trillion in taxes annually, the GAO said.
